thread.title: Dropbox: SMR Technology And A Lesson From Warren Buffett - Dropbox (NASDAQ:DBX)

author: Paulo Santos
title: Dropbox: SMR Technology And A Lesson From Warren Buffett - Dropbox (NASDAQ:DBX)
text:
The SMR of yore. Note the density improvements.
At times, the technology hyping gets too much. I don’t have a position or interest in Dropbox ( DBX ). I do find it, though, that Dropbox trades at a bubble valuation while:
Being in a very competitive marketplace where competitors are better positioned. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) integrates iCloud with iOS and MacOS. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ) integrates OneDrive with Windows and Office. Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) leads in deploying Google Drive among Android smartphones. Selling a commodity. Cloud storage space is a commodity. As a result of the above, Dropbox’s underlying business is hardly attractive. Yet, Dropbox trades at 129x 2018 consensus non-GAAP earnings. And here, a curiosity: These non-GAAP earnings come from excluding stock-based compensation as always. But in Dropbox’s case, the stock-based compensation is so high that it exceeds revenues (though this should be partially related to the recent IPO and thus will likely moderate going forward).
Still, the above is not what brings me here. This is not about valuation or how one arrives at that valuation. Instead, it’s about all the technology hype I’m reading when it comes to Dropbox.
At the forefront of this hype, is Dropbox’s deployment of “SMR Technology” in its “Magic Pocket” infrastructure:
SMR (Shingled Magnetic Recording) technology is a technology which takes into account that write heads on HDDs (Hard Disk Drives) are of a different size to read heads. So instead of basing the density of the information that’s written to the disk on the size of the write heads, this density is improved by taking into account the smaller size of the read head. This is done by partially overwriting past written information (by moving the write heads less than what would be required to fully clear the past written track). As for “Magic Pocket,” that’s simply a name given to Dropbox’s own cloud infrastructure – as Dropbox decided to go with its own data centers instead of buying space, on, say, Amazon’s (NASDAQ: AMZN ) AWS. Now, SMR technology promises greater data density, so higher capacities per HDD, so fewer HDDs for the same storage capacity, and more storage for the same data center square footage. This in turn can have several cost advantages at the data center level, and ultimately turn into higher efficiency and lower operational costs. SMR does have disadvantages, too. Namely:
It sacrifices the possibility of doing random writes. This is so because the process is only amenable to sequential writes … if a write head was to try and write again over the same space, it would partially destroy the “top shingles” (the tracks which were overlaid on the previously written tracks). It has lower (write) performance. To go around these limitations, and benefit from the density and cost advantages, Dropbox had to make many different adaptations to its storage architecture. A good read on these changes can be found here . These involved both changes to hardware, topology and software. With lots of care, especially on staging (memory, cache SSDs) before writing to the final SMR drives, Dropbox was thus able to use SMR without compromising performance (where performance is critical).
Finally, all those SMR drives are simply HDDs bought from suppliers. SMR itself is thus not some kind of Dropbox technology - it’s just something Dropbox buys. And the changes Dropbox had to implement to fully enjoy the cost benefits while avoiding the performance pitfalls were basically obvious to specialists working in the area (for Dropbox or anyone else).
So Where Does Warren Buffett Figure In All Of This? No, Warren Buffett isn’t there in the title for clickbait or something. There is a very specific reason why I named him. Let’s see:
All of the considerations above did not change the fact that providing cloud storage is a very competitive commodity business. If we include even just part of the SBC (Stock-Based Compensation) Dropbox ignores in its non-GAAP earnings, it’s an obviously low-margin business. They also don’t change the fact that any competitor (Google, Microsoft, Apple, Box (NYSE: BOX ), Amazon.com, etc) can use the exact same technology. Now, I’m going to quote Charlie Munger, which in turn quotes Warren Buffett, in a talk he gave back in 1994 :
The great lesson in microeconomics is to discriminate between when technology is going to help you and when it's going to kill you. And most people do not get this straight in their heads. But a fellow like Buffett does.
For example, when we were in the textile business, which is a terrible commodity business, we were making low-end textiles - which are a real commodity product. And one day, the people came to Warren and said, 'They've invented a new loom that we think will do twice as much work as our old ones.'
And Warren said, 'Gee, I hope this doesn't work because if it does, I'm going to close the mill.' And he meant it.
See what he said there? That new loom, with double the efficiency, is the SMR technology of today. So why would Warren Buffett have to “close the mill” on the face of such promising technology? The explanation is given right after:
What was he thinking? He was thinking, 'It's a lousy business. We're earning substandard returns and keeping it open just to be nice to the elderly workers. But we're not going to put huge amounts of new capital into a lousy business.'
And he knew that the huge productivity increases that would come from a better machine introduced into the production of a commodity product would all go to the benefit of the buyers of the textiles. Nothing was going to stick to our ribs as owners.
That's such an obvious concept - that there are all kinds of wonderful new inventions that give you nothing as owners except the opportunity to spend a lot more money in a business that's still going to be lousy. The money still won't come to you. All of the advantages from great improvements are going to flow through to the customers.
Hence, that’s the Warren Buffett insight on a similar issue. When we’re talking about a highly competitive commodity business, technology advances which increase your efficiency don’t necessarily improve your economics. They can even just represent another way to force investors to dump more money into the same ugly business.
Ultimately, the benefits of such technological advances flow to the end users, not to those applying new technologies made available by their suppliers.
Conclusion There are a few conclusions to be drawn here:
Dropbox is currently printing very nice free cash flow figures. This is mostly because its depreciation is much higher than its capex ($35.9 million vs $9.9 million in the latest quarter) and because of SBC as seen before. Were Dropbox to need to move massively into investing into these new drives and topology, and capex would shoot up, crippling FCF. However, since Dropbox is only targeting 25% of the capacity on SMR drives, Dropbox is probably aware of this and would only be aggressive if forced (by competitors). Given that SMR technology will allow for lower costs, and that the thesis above says these cheaper costs will be enjoyed by customers, we’re likely to see lower pricing for storage. That’s already been the case, of course, since this is hardly the only technological advance allowing for lower costs. Customers usually have significant inertia. As a result, rapidly falling costs can still benefit the company since customers won’t instantly shift toward a lower cost alternative. This would become worse if and when costs stopped going down. The parallel above, in Warren Buffett’s story, is that it would take a time for the cost savings to be passed on to customers, so there would be a temporary boost to margins even there – it just wouldn’t last long. The end business is growing rapidly. This means investment isn’t necessarily to replace already existing capacity to serve the same customers. This marries well with customer inertia, and allows more time to get returns on past investments. The problem would also be much more evident if growth was to slow down significantly. Anyway, it doesn’t make a whole lot of sense to price some kind of premium into Dropbox because of “SMR technology.”
